<reason>Both sides argued at a high level and both suffered symmetric clipping. PRO won by keeping a single decision rule in view ("when 'Buy' turns out to be a lie, who eats the loss?") and by resolving CON's best pressure cleanly: the "if switchable it isn't a guarantee" dilemma was answered with the house analogy (a guarantee binds the seller's boilerplate, not the dead owner), and CON's "labeling already delivers this" was punctured with the floor-vs-menu distinction—CON's own framing made designation something platforms "may sell," so existing libraries remain a windfall. CON landed real damage (defaults bite the unprepared; sublicensing limits what retailers can promise; ownership-of-a-file vs. dependency-on-a-server), but CON's answer to PRO's Q2—restitution/damages for a grieving widow—was a visible weak point PRO exploited memorably, and CON's closing leaned on an unsupported assertion that the guarantee binds only future sales. PRO's minor flaws (a nonexistent [C1.x] reference, premature claim of CON "silence" due to turn order) did not offset its cleaner path. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 2 answering CON's Q2: "Yes, a buyer can switch it off... 'Guarantee' means the platform cannot strip the right by boilerplate; it does not mean the dead are compelled... You are guaranteed the right to leave your house to whomever you choose," followed by "A guarantee is a floor; a label is a menu the seller writes"—this dissolved CON's dilemma and exposed the optionality in CON's alternative.</best_rebuttal>
